title: Terahertz Time-Domain Spectroscopy as a Universal Defect Fingerprinting Tool for Organic Halide Perovskite Solar Cells
authors: Inhee Maeng, Young Mi Lee, Jinwoo Park, Seung Jae Oh, Min-Cherl Jung
abstract: Organic-inorganic hybrid perovskites (OHPs) deliver certified single-junction power conversion efficiencies (PCEs) exceeding 26% and perovskite-silicon tandem values surpassing 34%, yet a substantial gap with the Shockley-Queisser (S-Q) limit persists-primarily due to grain-boundary (GB) defects that drive non-radiative recombination, ion migration, and degradation. Rational passivation demands a non-contact tool capable of identifying and quantifying specific defect species in device-relevant thin films, a capability absent from conventional probes. This short review demonstrates that terahertz time-domain spectroscopy (THz-TDS, 0.3-3.0 THz) fulfills this role. Across four OHP compositions fabricated by sequential vacuum evaporation (SVE)-MAPbI3, MAPbBr3, FAPbI3, and CsPbI3-the THz spectral window captures both intrinsic phonon modes and GB-localized molecular defect vibrations, enabling species-specific, quantitative characterization at room temperature. Notably, the oscillator strength of the SVE-specific 1.58 THz absorption in MAPbI3 scales linearly with XPS-quantified CH3NH2 defect concentration, establishing THz-TDS as a direct, non-destructive defect meter. Building on these findings, we propose a three-pillar framework for THz-guided defect engineering: (I) quantitative defect measurement via oscillator-strength analysis, (II) material-specific fingerprint identification from a systematically constructed THz library, and (III) fingerprint-guided defect elimination with real-time feedback-together defining a closed-loop quality-control cycle that connects spectroscopic diagnosis to passivation strategy and, ultimately, to enhanced solar-cell efficiency.

infographic.key_insight: Terahertz time-domain spectroscopy can directly fingerprint and quantify grain-boundary defect species in organic halide perovskite thin films using room-temperature spectral signatures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a non-contact diagnostic for closed-loop defect passivation and quality control in perovskite solar-cell manufacturing.
method: Measure 0.3–3.0 THz spectra of SVE-fabricated OHP films.
Match intrinsic phonon peaks and GB-localized defect vibrations to a THz fingerprint library.
Use oscillator-strength analysis to quantify defect concentration and guide passivation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the 1.58 THz absorption in MAPbI3 scales linearly with XPS-quantified CH3NH2 defect concentration across four perovskite compositions.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on building reliable material-specific THz reference libraries and may be sensitive to film fabrication, thickness, and measurement conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Terahertz Time-Domain Spectroscopy as a Universal Defect Fingerprinting Tool for Organic Halide Perovskite Solar Cells

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning-Based Energy Management for Hydrogen-Enabled Community Microgrids Under Uncertainty
authors: Mohamed Atef, Sanath Alahakoon, Umme Mumtahina, Peter Wolfs, Tamer Khatib, Moslem Uddin
abstract: Hydrogen-enabled community microgrids can improve renewable energy utilization and local resilience, but their operation is complicated by intermittent generation, uncertain residential demand, dynamic electricity prices, and the coupled dynamics of battery and hydrogen storage. This paper develops a proximal policy optimization (PPO)-based energy management system (EMS) for a grid-connected community microgrid integrating photovoltaic and wind generation, battery storage, an electrolyzer, hydrogen storage, a fuel cell, and diesel backup. The EMS is formulated as a Markov decision process with an 11-dimensional state and three continuous control actions for battery, diesel, and hydrogen dispatch; grid exchange is determined from the residual power balance. The framework is evaluated using 8,760 hourly observations for a 1,000-household community in Rockhampton, Australia. Under the normal operating scenario, the learned policy produced a net annual operating revenue of A$195,690.67, a renewable fraction of 91.2%, a carbon intensity of 0.085 kg CO2/kWh under the adopted accounting boundary, and 99.77% load satisfaction. With the hourly grid-outage probability increased from 1% to 5%, the policy retained A$169,892.21 in net operating revenue and supplied 98.79% of demand, supported by a 413% increase in battery discharge and a 429% increase in diesel generation. The results demonstrate the potential of PPO for coordinated battery-hydrogen dispatch while also highlighting sensitivity to renewable-profile variability, training stability, and the choice of evaluation boundary.

infographic.key_insight: A PPO-based controller can coordinate battery, hydrogen, diesel, and grid exchange in a community microgrid to maximize revenue while maintaining very high load satisfaction under uncertainty.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work shows how reinforcement learning can improve operational scheduling of hybrid renewable microgrids, especially where storage coupling and variable prices make rule-based control inefficient.
method: Formulated EMS as an 11-state Markov decision process
Used PPO with three continuous actions for battery, diesel, and hydrogen dispatch
Evaluated grid-connected operation with PV, wind, battery, electrolyzer, H2 storage, fuel cell, and diesel backup
infographic.evidence_signal: The policy was tested on 8,760 hourly observations for a 1,000-household community and achieved A$195,690.67 annual operating revenue, 91.2% renewable fraction, and 99.77% load satisfaction in the base case.
infographic.watch_item: Performance is sensitive to renewable-profile variability and training stability, so real deployment would need robust retraining and careful validation across operating boundaries.
infographic.paper_title: Deep Reinforcement Learning-Based Energy Management for Hydrogen-Enabled Community Microgrids Under Uncertainty

title: Symbolic Predicate-Guided Language Agents for Inverse Design of Perovskite Oxides
authors: Dong Hyeon Mok, Seoin Back, Victor Fung, Guoxiang Hu
abstract: Efficient discovery of high-performance materials has been pursued through a variety of data- and AI-driven strategies, among which inverse design, generating materials from desired target properties, has emerged as an important paradigm. Large language models (LLMs) offer a complementary route for inverse materials design because their reasoning and in-context learning capability can be used not only to propose candidates but also to demonstrate interpretable design principles. In this work, we introduce a domain specific language (DSL)-guided strategy to improve the reasoning and design capability of LLM agents by translating natural language design rules into symbolic predicates encoded in a predefined chemistry DSL. These predicates allow the LLM agent to obtain statistical evidence from the accumulated materials data, enabling the agent to evaluate and refine its own reasoning during the design loop. Based on this strategy, we developed a multi-agent materials design framework, called Operational Rule-grounded CHEmical Search Through Reasoning Agents (ORCHESTRA), and applied it to the inverse design of double perovskite oxides under multiple target-property objectives. The results show that symbolic predicates help the LLM identify unsupported rules, validate newly proposed rules and improve the rule store over iterative design cycles. Compared with a strategy relying only on natural language rules, the DSL-guided framework showed the potential to improve materials design performance, particularly for challenging target properties. These findings suggest that mathematical and statistical grounding can enhance the reasoning capability of LLM agents in materials science and that LLM-based inverse design can be performed effectively without large task-specific datasets or additional model training.

infographic.key_insight: A DSL-guided multi-agent LLM framework grounds materials-design rules in symbolic predicates, helping the agent reason more reliably for inverse design of double perovskite oxides.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach suggests a practical path to AI-assisted materials discovery that can improve candidate generation and rule validation without requiring large task-specific training datasets.
method: Translate natural-language design rules into chemistry DSL predicates
Use accumulated materials data to provide statistical evidence for or against rules
Iteratively refine candidate designs and the rule store with a multi-agent ORCHESTRA loop
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that, versus natural-language rules alone, the DSL-guided framework improved validation of unsupported rules and showed better potential for challenging target properties in double perovskite inverse design.
infographic.watch_item: Performance gains are described as potential rather than fully quantified in the abstract, so the approach still needs careful benchmarking and domain-specific validation before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Symbolic Predicate-Guided Language Agents for Inverse Design of Perovskite Oxides

title: A Digital Twin-Based Method for Evaluating Local Collective Tariffs in Distribution-Level Energy Systems
authors: Kristoffer Christensen, Bo Nørregaard Jørgensen, Zheng Grace Ma
abstract: This work addresses the need for engineering-grounded evaluation of implement-ed tariff mechanisms in distribution-level energy systems. A digital twin-based method is proposed for assessing local collective tariffs under realistic behavioral and infrastructural conditions. The approach integrates agent-based modeling of household consumption and generation, virtual aggregation through a shared metering abstraction, and explicit representation of tariff logic within a unified simulation environment. The method is demonstrated through its application to the Danish Local Collective Tariff across representative residential energy community configurations, including scenarios with photovoltaic generation, battery storage, and electric vehicle charging. Results indicate that aggregation of heterogeneous demand profiles reduces peak coincidence and enables more efficient allocation of tariff components, leading to measurable cost reductions at the community level. At the same time, the outcomes reveal sensitivity to the temporal alignment of consumption and generation, influencing the degree of cost neutrality across participants. The findings illustrate how digital twin-based evaluation can support systematic assessment of tariff mechanisms by capturing the interaction between infrastructure, user behavior, and regulatory design. The proposed approach provides a basis for analyzing and comparing tariff structures in distribution-level energy systems beyond the specific case considered.

infographic.key_insight: A digital twin can evaluate local collective tariffs by simulating household behavior, shared metering, and tariff rules under realistic distribution-grid conditions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method gives engineers a practical way to test whether tariff designs reduce community costs while remaining fair and operationally plausible for residential energy communities.
method: Agent-based modeling of household load, PV generation, batteries, and EV charging
Virtual aggregation through a shared metering abstraction
Explicit tariff logic embedded in one simulation environment
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports application to Danish Local Collective Tariff scenarios and finds measurable community-level cost reductions from aggregation of heterogeneous demand profiles.
infographic.watch_item: Cost neutrality can vary with the temporal alignment of consumption and generation, so tariff outcomes may be sensitive to participant behavior and local asset timing.
infographic.paper_title: A Digital Twin-Based Method for Evaluating Local Collective Tariffs in Distribution-Level Energy Systems

title: Superconductivity in MgHCu3 perovskite revisited
authors: Piotr Szkudlarek, Wojciech Grochala
abstract: We reexamine the crystal structure, electronic structure, lattice dynamics, phonon dispersion, electron-phonon coupling, and superconducting properties of MgHCu3 perovskite using the PBEsol and PBE functionals. This perovskite phase was recently proposed to exhibit superconductivity with the critical superconducting temperature, TC, of 42 K, which falls slightly over the classical 40 K limit for the phonon driven superconductivity. We show that although the crystal and electronic structure of this hypothetical compound are quite robust with respect to the k point mesh and functional used, yet the phonons and phonon related properties are extremely sensitive to the density of the grid chosen as well as functional used for calculations. Correspondingly, the values of the critical superconducting temperature calculated here for different Gaussian broadenings vary in a broad range of ca. 10 to 31 K and they do not exceed the classical limit. We suggest that the properties of this and many other high TC hydrides claimed should be thoroughly scrutinized using a variety of functionals, and benchmarked with experiment, to provide more reliable values of TC.

infographic.key_insight: Revisiting MgHCu3 with two DFT functionals shows that its predicted superconductivity is much less robust than previously claimed, with Tc falling below the classical 40 K limit.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The study highlights that superconductivity predictions for hypothetical perovskites/hydrides can be highly sensitive to computational setup, so design decisions should be validated across methods before materials screening claims are trusted.
method: Reexamined crystal structure and electronic structure with PBEsol and PBE.
Calculated lattice dynamics, phonon dispersion, and electron-phonon coupling.
Compared sensitivity to k-point mesh density, functional choice, and Gaussian broadening.
infographic.evidence_signal: While the crystal and electronic structure remained stable, phonons and related properties changed strongly with numerical settings, and the computed Tc ranged from about 10 to 31 K.
infographic.watch_item: Predicted superconducting performance is highly method-dependent, so claims for this material should not be treated as reliable without cross-functional checks and experimental benchmarking.
infographic.paper_title: Superconductivity in MgHCu3 perovskite revisited

title: Human and LLM Collaboration for Accelerated Materials Synthesis and Discovery
authors: Gregory Bassen, Wyatt Bunstine, Sarah Okandey, Sarah Cheung, Elaine Flowers, Ritwik Bose
abstract: Although Large Language Models (LLM) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools have enabled a rapid increase in the generation rate of predicted materials, the rate of new materials discovery has lagged behind. This is due to the challenges associated with designing a sequence of chemical reactions to predictably produce new materials, especially in new structure types. Here, we report a study of human and LLM generated recipes for the synthesis of known and new materials. The success of the recipes is determined through in-lab experimentation, and the results are passed back to the humans and LLMs in a closed-loop process to study the effects of their collaboration. The Ruddlesden-Popper homologous series was selected for all material candidates to provide a materials phase space that is simultaneously well studied and likely to host undiscovered materials. We find that humans (H) and LLM (L) have similar success rates: 83(8)% (H) and 75(9)% (L) [known materials, round one], 17(9)% (H) and 22(10)% (L) [unknown materials, round one], 79(8)% (H) and 71(9)% (L) [known materials, round two], and 22(7)% (H) and 14(6)% (L) [unknown materials, round two]. Through this collaborative human-LLM effort, we discovered Ba3PtO5, a material with a new structural prototype that constitutes the missing 1D member of the herein reported dimensionally tunable Rock-Salt Perovskite (RSP) homologous series of the form (AX)m(ABX3)p, of which the Ruddlesden-Popper series is a subset.

infographic.key_insight: Human and LLM collaboration can accelerate materials synthesis by generating experimentally testable recipes, and it can even reveal previously unknown structures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A closed-loop human–LLM workflow offers a practical route to speed up materials discovery and synthesis planning for next-generation functional materials.
method: Human and LLMs independently proposed synthesis recipes for known and unknown materials in the Ruddlesden-Popper family.
Recipes were executed in the lab and success was evaluated experimentally.
Results were fed back into a closed-loop process for a second round of collaboration.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across two rounds, humans and LLMs achieved similar lab success rates on known materials (83% vs 75% in round one; 79% vs 71% in round two) and lower but nonzero success on unknown targets (17% vs 22%; 22% vs 14%), enabling discovery of Ba3PtO5.
infographic.watch_item: Success on unknown materials remained modest, so lab validation and careful chemistry constraints are still essential before relying on generated recipes.
infographic.paper_title: Human and LLM Collaboration for Accelerated Materials Synthesis and Discovery

title: The WEST code for large-scale excited-state materials simulations
authors: Victor Wen-zhe Yu, Siyuan Chen, Yu Jin, Vrindaa Somjit, Stefano Paolo Villani, Jiawei Zhan
abstract: We present WEST, an open-source plane-wave pseudopotential code for large-scale excited-state materials simulations, and describe its theoretical foundations, software architecture, and capabilities. WEST implements full-frequency GW, quantum defect embedding theory, the Bethe-Salpeter equation, and time-dependent density functional theory within a common algorithmic framework that avoids the explicit computation of virtual electronic states. By combining density functional and density matrix perturbation theory, low-rank representations of the dielectric screening and exact exchange, and localization techniques, WEST achieves favorable computational scaling with system size. The code supports the calculation of quasi-particle and neutral excitation energies, optical and photoluminescence spectra, excited-state forces, and non-adiabatic couplings, with interoperable workflows connecting to quantum chemistry, vibronic coupling, and quantum computing packages. A hierarchical parallelization strategy and GPU acceleration deliver near-ideal strong scaling to thousands of GPUs, enabling accurate excited-state simulations of systems with more than a thousand atoms. Representative applications, spanning the full optical cycle of solid-state spin defects, self-trapped excitons in metal-halide perovskites, and the optical response of liquid water and ice, demonstrate the accuracy and versatility of the code across diverse material classes. The capabilities implemented in WEST establish the code as a scalable platform for predictive excited-state simulations, high-throughput materials discovery, and the generation of high-fidelity datasets for machine learning in computational materials science.

infographic.key_insight: WEST is a scalable open-source platform for excited-state simulations that combines GW, Bethe-Salpeter, TDDFT, and embedding methods without explicit virtual states.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For solar-cell and materials engineering, it enables practical prediction of optical excitations, quasiparticle energies, and excited-state dynamics in large, realistic systems such as perovskites.
method: Full-frequency GW and Bethe-Salpeter equation for quasiparticle and neutral excitations
TDDFT and quantum defect embedding in a common no-virtual-states framework
Hierarchical parallelization, GPU acceleration, and low-rank screening/exchange representations
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports near-ideal strong scaling to thousands of GPUs and successful applications to systems with more than a thousand atoms, including self-trapped excitons in metal-halide perovskites.
infographic.watch_item: Performance and accuracy depend on sophisticated implementations and high-performance hardware, so workflow complexity may limit adoption in smaller computational environments.
infographic.paper_title: The WEST code for large-scale excited-state materials simulations

title: High-entropy perovskites, architectured by s0/d0/d10 cations, as novel electrolytes for solid oxide fuel cells
authors: Ho Truong Nam Hai, Rishad Kunafiev, Kwati Leonard, Kaveh Edalati
abstract: Solid oxide fuel cells enable efficient conversion of hydrogen into electricity. However, the limited availability of materials for their cathode, anode, and electrolyte remains a concern. This study introduces three high-entropy oxide perovskites as novel electrolyte materials for fuel cells (Ba0.50Sr0.50)(Ti0.33Zr0.33Hf0.33)O3 with s0/d0 cations, (Ba0.50Sr0.50)(Ga0.33In0.33Sn0.33)O3 with s0/d10 cations, and (Ba0.50Sr0.50)(Ti0.33Zr0.33Sn0.33)O3 with mixed s0/d0/d10 cations. Through sequential sintering by high-pressure torsion processing and calcination, these perovskites were synthesized and then printed with a thickness of about 6-10 microns on a Ni-SrZr0.5Ce0.4Y0.1O3 substrate as an anode and then coated with Ba0.5La0.5CoO3 as a cathode. Electrochemical analysis and impedance spectroscopy show that (Ba0.50Sr0.50)(Ti0.33Zr0.33Sn0.33)O3 with s0/d0/d10 cations exhibits the best performance with negligible current leakage and lowest ohmic resistance, while its maximum power density reaches 0.53 W.cm-2 at 973 K. Complementary synchrotron X-ray absorption and photoelectron spectroscopy analyses indicate that the superior performance of (Ba0.50Sr0.50)(Ti0.33Zr0.33Sn0.33)O3 correlates with its heterogeneous electronic structure characterized by tailored unoccupied d-orbital states, and favorable local metal-oxygen bond lengths and extrinsic oxygen vacancies. This investigation demonstrates the significance of high-entropy perovskites with mixed s0/d0/d10 cations as new rare-earth metal-free ion-conducting electrolytes, particularly for protonic solid oxide fuel cells.

infographic.key_insight: A mixed s0/d0/d10 high-entropy perovskite electrolyte, (Ba0.50Sr0.50)(Ti0.33Zr0.33Sn0.33)O3, delivered the best solid oxide fuel cell performance by combining low leakage, low ohmic resistance, and favorable oxygen-ion/proton-conducting structure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This work expands the electrolyte design space for solid oxide fuel cells by enabling rare-earth-free, high-entropy perovskite ceramics with improved conductivity and device power output.
method: Synthesized three high-entropy perovskite electrolytes via sequential sintering, high-pressure torsion processing, and calcination.
Printed ~6–10 μm electrolyte films on Ni–SrZr0.5Ce0.4Y0.1O3 anodes and coated Ba0.5La0.5CoO3 cathodes.
Compared electrochemical behavior with impedance spectroscopy plus synchrotron XAS and XPS to link structure with performance.
infographic.evidence_signal: The mixed s0/d0/d10 composition achieved the best result, with negligible current leakage, the lowest ohmic resistance, and a maximum power density of 0.53 W·cm−2 at 973 K.
infographic.watch_item: The reported performance is promising but still depends on careful control of microstructure, film thickness, and high-temperature processing, which may affect reproducibility and scale-up.
infographic.paper_title: High-entropy perovskites, architectured by s0/d0/d10 cations, as novel electrolytes for solid oxide fuel cells

title: Photovoltaics beyond the panel: system-level net energy under grid and firming constraints
authors: Hans Peter Beck
abstract: Photovoltaics can exhibit favourable installation-level energy return on investment (EROI), yet electricity must also be delivered when solar and wind generation are insufficient. This study evaluates how the energy balance changes when the boundary is expanded to reliable electricity supply. A fleet-equivalent benchmark model includes component turnover, grids, storage, renewable overbuild, dispatchable backup, and fuel supply. It is not a simulation, optimization, or real-system prediction. Photovoltaics provide the accounting reference in an illustrative Central European mix of 80% wind and 20% photovoltaics, while the firming penalties arise more generally from weather-dependent generation. Expanding the boundary is decisive. The unfirmed renewable fleet retains an EROI of 10.7-16.0, but does not provide continuous electricity. Battery load-balancing references decline from 7.1-12.5 for 1h to 0.7-2.3 for 24h. Seasonal hydrogen yields 3.4-7.7; adding a 1h battery reduces the combined range to 2.9-6.8. Pipeline-gas and LNG backup yield only 1.2-2.6 and 1.0-2.2. The lifecycle-carbon advantage narrows accordingly. Under present industrial supply chains, GWP$_{100}$ intensities rise from 38-75 gCO$_2$eq/kWh without firming to 80-289 gCO$_2$eq/kWh for hydrogen and battery-hydrogen firming, and 121-327 gCO$_2$eq/kWh for gas backup. These favourable benchmarks set orientation, site, curtailment, and delivery factors to unity; real deployment lowers EROI and raises emissions. The results identify firming as a critical energetic constraint: reliable decarbonization requires firm low-carbon generation with sufficient net-energy surplus to sustain a resilient industrial society.

infographic.key_insight: Photovoltaics look strongly net-positive at the panel level, but their energy return drops sharply once reliable, always-available electricity delivery is included.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The paper shows that grid integration, storage, overbuild, and backup requirements can dominate system-level net energy and emissions, so firming strategy is a core design constraint for low-carbon power systems.
method: Fleet-equivalent benchmark accounting model
Includes component turnover, grids, storage, overbuild, dispatchable backup, and fuel supply
Compares unfirmed renewables with battery, hydrogen, and gas firming scenarios
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports benchmark EROI ranges and GWP100 intensities across firming options in an illustrative Central European wind-PV mix, using an accounting framework rather than a predictive simulation.
infographic.watch_item: The results are illustrative benchmark values with favorable assumptions set to unity, so real deployments will typically have lower EROI and higher emissions.
infographic.paper_title: Photovoltaics beyond the panel: system-level net energy under grid and firming constraints

title: LLMs for Agentic Home Energy Management
authors: Sokipriala Jonah
abstract: Home Energy Management Systems (HEMS) can reduce residential electricity costs and support demand response, but adoption is limited by the difficulty of translating household preferences into technical scheduling constraints. This paper evaluates whether large language model (LLM) agents can provide a practical natural-language interface for multi-appliance home energy scheduling. We present a tool-calling ReAct agent that uses live half-hourly Octopus Agile prices, weather forecasts, photovoltaic generation estimates, household usage data, and a retrieval-augmented knowledge base to schedule flexible loads against a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) ground truth. Three commercial models, GPT-4o-mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and Claude Sonnet 4.6, are benchmarked across tariff days, constraint-conflict scenarios, weather-aware solar co-optimization, and week-long deployment. With native function calling, all models achieve 100% scheduling success and near-MILP optimality, while text-parsed action interfaces sharply reduce reliability. Constraint testing shows that cost-optimal and safety-optimal models differ: Claude is strongest under infeasibility and power-cap conflicts, while GPT-4o-mini is most efficient. Over a simulated week, agents capture 96.7-98.0% of oracle savings, projecting approximately GBP 1,270 annual savings over an off-peak timer baseline. Code and a live demonstration are available at https://github.com/sokistar24/ecohome-energy-agent and https://www.ecohomeagent.com/.

infographic.key_insight: LLM agents can translate natural-language household preferences into near-optimal home energy schedules, achieving reliable multi-appliance optimization when paired with native tool calling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables a practical natural-language control layer for Home Energy Management Systems that can reduce electricity costs while handling tariffs, solar generation, weather, and appliance constraints.
method: Tool-calling ReAct agent for scheduling flexible home loads
Uses live Octopus Agile prices, weather forecasts, PV estimates, usage data, and a retrieval-augmented knowledge base
Benchmarked against MILP ground truth across tariff, conflict, and week-long deployment scenarios
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three commercial LLMs, native function calling yielded 100% scheduling success and 96.7–98.0% of oracle savings over a simulated week.
infographic.watch_item: Performance drops sharply with text-parsed action interfaces, so robust function-calling integration and constraint handling are critical for deployment.
infographic.paper_title: LLMs for Agentic Home Energy Management

title: Robustness of Reinforcement Learning-Based Congestion Management in Low-Voltage Grids
authors: Josef Hoppe, Sarra Bouchkati, Farah Nasr, Jonathan Krapp, Alexander Och, Maximilian Wirth
abstract: Increases in photovoltaic generation, charging of electric vehicles and heat-pump demand challenge operating limits in low-voltage distribution grids. This requires curative curtailment methods that can operate under sparse observability, noisy measurements, and imperfect grid models. Unlike prior end-to-end reinforcement-learning approaches for partially observable curtailment, this work decouples congestion detection and control by combining a random-forest violation pre-classifier with an actor-critic controller, and evaluates its robustness to measurement noise and grid-parameter mismatch. The framework is tested on a real low-voltage grid using synthetic future operating scenarios with low observability and controllability. With accurate grid parameters, the controller reduces total violation magnitude by 98.9%, and this performance remains nearly unchanged under the tested measurement-noise settings. Grid-model mismatch proves to be more challenging, but the controller still mitigates most violations under the tested mismatch assumptions.

infographic.key_insight: A decoupled reinforcement-learning pipeline with a random-forest congestion detector and actor-critic controller can robustly reduce low-voltage grid violations under sparse observability.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This approach is relevant for managing PV-rich distribution grids with EV and heat-pump loads, where curative curtailment must work despite noisy measurements and imperfect grid models.
method: Random-forest pre-classifier flags likely voltage/current violations.
Actor-critic controller decides curtailment actions only when congestion is predicted.
Robustness is tested against measurement noise and grid-parameter mismatch on a real low-voltage grid.
infographic.evidence_signal: On a real low-voltage grid with synthetic future operating scenarios, the controller reduced total violation magnitude by 98.9% with accurate parameters and remained nearly unchanged under the tested noise levels.
infographic.watch_item: Performance is more sensitive to grid-model mismatch than to measurement noise, so deployment still requires careful parameter validation and model updating.
infographic.paper_title: Robustness of Reinforcement Learning-Based Congestion Management in Low-Voltage Grids

title: SevenNet-Polar for MultiTask Prediction of Energy, Forces, Stress, and Born Effective Charges: Development and Application to ZrO$_2$, Li$_3$PO$_4$, and Perovskites
authors: Anh Khoa Augustin Lu, Shungo Arai, Yutack Park, Seungwu Han, Tsuyoshi Miyazaki, Satoshi Watanabe
abstract: Accurate prediction of the Born effective charge (BEC) tensor is crucial for modeling materials under electric fields but remains computationally expensive. To bridge this gap, we present SevenNet-Polar, an equivariant graph neural network framework based on the SevenNet architecture for fast and accurate BEC predictions. Our BEC-only predictors can achieve an RMSE as low as 0.0043 e on ZrO$_2$, Li$_3$PO$_4$, and perovskites, despite the presence of high-temperature (up to 2,000 K) and defect-laden training data. Our all-in-one multitask models for predicting energy, forces, stress, and BEC in ZrO$_2$ and Li$_3$PO$_4$ achieve high accuracy with an RMSE of 1.0 meV/atom for energy, 12 meV/angstrom for forces, 0.05 GPa for stress, and 0.0029 e for BEC. BEC accuracy is not degraded by multitask training. Scaling analysis reveals distinct exponents for diagonal and off-diagonal BEC components, both of which exhibit less favorable scaling than energy, force and stress errors. SevenNet-Polar generalizes robustly when tested on scenarios containing structural environments absent from the training set, such as along nudged elastic band (NEB) trajectories or grain boundaries in ZrO$_2$. Accelerated by FlashTP, SevenNet-Polar enables simulations containing up to 1.5 million atoms on multi-GPU supercomputers and up to approximately 15,000 atoms on a single consumer-grade GPU. This makes charge-aware molecular dynamics simulations under electric fields more accessible.

infographic.key_insight: SevenNet-Polar extends an equivariant GNN to predict Born effective charges alongside energy, forces, and stress with near-DFT accuracy, enabling faster charge-aware simulations under electric fields.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This makes high-throughput screening and molecular dynamics for ferroelectrics, oxides, and perovskite solar-cell materials much more practical at scale.
method: Built on the SevenNet equivariant graph neural network framework
Trained multitask models for energy, forces, stress, and Born effective charges
Used FlashTP acceleration to run large-scale simulations on single- and multi-GPU systems
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports BEC RMSE as low as 0.0043 e for BEC-only models and 0.0029 e in multitask models, with energy/force/stress errors of 1.0 meV/atom, 12 meV/Å, and 0.05 GPa.
infographic.watch_item: BEC scaling is less favorable than energy/force/stress and the model should still be checked carefully on environments far outside the training set.
infographic.paper_title: SevenNet-Polar for MultiTask Prediction of Energy, Forces, Stress, and Born Effective Charges: Development and Application to ZrO$_2$, Li$_3$PO$_4$, and Perovskites

title: Hyperfine driven spin relaxation of charge carriers in metal-halide perovskites
authors: Guillaume Lague, Frédérick Bernardot, Mauricio Calvo, Olfa Selmi, Sofia Masi, Christophe Testelin
abstract: Spin relaxation of localized charge carriers in semiconductors is primarily governed by hyperfine interaction with the surrounding nuclear spin bath. While this mechanism is well-established in III-V bulk materials and quantum dots, its critical role in metal halide perovskites (MHPs) has only recently emerged. Their inverted band structure induces an unusual hierarchy of hyperfine couplings, with hole interactions dominating electron interactions, particurlaly in Pb-based perovskites. Here, we adapt a spin relaxation model - originally developed for muon spin spectroscopy - to provide an exact description of longitudinal spin relaxation for localized carriers across arbitrary hyperfine correlation times. This approach is motivated by recent experimental evidence in MAPbI3, which places carrier spins in an intermediate correlation regime, where conventional mono-exponential approximations fail. Our analysis reveals distinct hyperfine relaxation channels: electrons couple primarily to halogen nuclei, whereas holes are governed by metal nuclei. This leads to a key prediction - perovskites with lighter halogens and metal cations exhibit significantly extended spin lifetimes. Applied to time-resolved Faraday rotation data obtained from two perovskite samples, our model extracts key microscopic parameters - including the carrier localization volume and hyperfine correlation time - demonstrating the necessity of the exact dynamical solution over a single-exponential approximation. These findings provide microscopic insight into hyperfine-driven spin relaxation in MHPs and establish a robust framework for characterizing carrier localization and spin dynamics.

infographic.key_insight: Localized carrier spins in metal-halide perovskites relax through hyperfine coupling in an unusual way: electrons mainly interact with halogen nuclei, while holes are dominated by metal nuclei, and an exact dynamical model is needed in the intermediate regime.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Understanding which nuclei control spin relaxation can guide perovskite composition choices to prolong carrier spin lifetimes and improve spin-sensitive optoelectronic designs.
method: Adapted a muon spin relaxation model to localized carrier spins in perovskites.
Solved longitudinal spin relaxation exactly across arbitrary hyperfine correlation times.
Fit time-resolved Faraday rotation data to extract localization volume and correlation time.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model was applied to time-resolved Faraday rotation data from two perovskite samples and showed that a single-exponential approximation is inadequate in the experimentally relevant regime.
infographic.watch_item: The framework targets localized carriers and requires the correct correlation-time regime and material parameters, so it may not transfer directly to delocalized or strongly non-hyperfine-dominated systems.
infographic.paper_title: Hyperfine driven spin relaxation of charge carriers in metal-halide perovskites

title: Boosting Perovskite Light-Emitting Diodes Performance by Introducing High Work-function Metal Transition Layer
authors: Laixiang Qin
abstract: We investigated the impact of the anode's work-function on the performance of an all inorganic PeLED device which was hailed for stability and long lifetime with drift-diffusion and Poisson equations embedded as a computation package in Setfos, a commercially professional software to emulate LED. According to the simulation results, a conclusion that a thin high work-function metal layer inserted between indium tin oxide (ITO) and hole transport layer of nickel oxide (NiOx) substantially facilitated hole injection by decrementing the hole injection barrier. 2 nm thick gold (Au) had been checked and dramatically enhanced luminance intensity by more than 18 fold times had been attained. The situation went for other high work function metals like Pd and Pt as well. Our high work-function thin metal layers decorating anodes in PeLED in facilitating hole injection unfolds a new trajectory towards efficiently boosting PeLED luminance with a technique that is compatible with large scale fabrication process.

infographic.key_insight: A thin high work-function metal interlayer between ITO and NiOx lowers the hole-injection barrier and strongly boosts all-inorganic PeLED luminance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This is a scalable anode-engineering strategy that can improve charge injection and device brightness without changing the core perovskite stack.
method: Simulated device physics with drift-diffusion and Poisson equations in Setfos.
Inserted ultrathin high work-function metals between ITO and the hole transport layer.
Compared Au, Pd, and Pt interlayers for hole-injection improvement.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that a 2 nm Au interlayer increased luminance by more than 18× in simulation, with similar trends for Pd and Pt.
infographic.watch_item: The result is simulation-based, so real-device performance, interlayer continuity, and fabrication reproducibility still need experimental validation.
infographic.paper_title: Boosting Perovskite Light-Emitting Diodes Performance by Introducing High Work-function Metal Transition Layer

title: Sustainable photocatalytic CO2 conversion using microalgae as a carbon-negative scavenger
authors: Ho Truong Nam Hai, Augusto Ducati Luchessi, Makoto Arita, Qixin Guo, Kaveh Edalati
abstract: Photocatalytic CO2 conversion driven by solar energy is a highly promising approach in addressing rising atmospheric CO2 levels; however, its practical application remains limited by low conversion efficiency. In this study, a new strategy to enhance CO2 reduction toward CO and CH4 is proposed through the employment of microalgae as a sacrificial agent, and the efficiency is compared with conventional CO2 conversion without and with the use of microplastics as sacrificial agents. To realize this strategy, an AB2O6-type high-entropy oxide (HEO), (Cs1/7Ba4/7Bi2/7)(Nb1/2Ta1/2)2O6, with bi-polymorphy of layered perovskite and pyrochlore, is rationally designed. The HEO incorporates alkali metal cesium and alkaline earth metal barium to increase surface basicity for CO2 chemisorption, bismuth with its stereochemically active lone pairs for localized polarization and charge separation, and tantalum and niobium to form octahedral crystalline frameworks for charge transport. The utilization of microalgae during photocatalytic reactions leads to a remarkable enhancement in CO2 conversion compared to catalysis with or without using microplastics, with CO and CH4 production increasing by 10- and 4-fold, respectively, compared to the system using only HEO. These findings not only demonstrate a new family of polymorphic AB2-type HEOs for photocatalysis but also show the potential of microalgae as a sustainable sacrificial agent, offering an environmentally friendly pathway for efficient CO2 capture (through photosynthesis by microalgae) and CO2 conversion (through photocatalysis by HEOs).

infographic.key_insight: A polymorphic high-entropy oxide photocatalyst combined with microalgae sacrificial scavenging substantially boosts solar-driven CO2 conversion to CO and CH4.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work suggests a scalable, low-toxicity route to improve photocatalytic carbon utilization by tuning catalyst composition and pairing it with a carbon-negative biological co-reagent.
method: Designed AB2O6-type HEO (Cs1/7Ba4/7Bi2/7)(Nb1/2Ta1/2)2O6 with layered perovskite/pyrochlore bi-polymorphy.
Used Cs and Ba to increase surface basicity, Bi to promote polarization/charge separation, and Nb/Ta octahedra for charge transport.
Compared CO2 photoconversion using the HEO alone, with microplastics, and with microalgae as sacrificial agents.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that microalgae increased CO and CH4 production by about 10× and 4×, respectively, relative to the HEO-only system.
infographic.watch_item: Practical implementation will need verification of long-term stability, light-to-fuel efficiency, and whether microalgae supply/handling remains feasible at scale.
infographic.paper_title: Sustainable photocatalytic CO2 conversion using microalgae as a carbon-negative scavenger

title: Role of small-radius and high-electronegativity A-Site dopants in enhancing proton transport and stability of perovskite electrolytes
authors: Hang Ma, Ying Liang, Tianxing Ma
abstract: The practical application of BaCeO$_3$-based electrolytes is limited by their poor chemical stability in proton-conducting solid oxide fuel cells. Commonly employed B-site doping strategies typically improve proton transport with limited improvement in stability. Recent experiments show that A-site Ca doping can simultaneously enhance both properties. Here, through first-principles calculations and mechanistic analysis of Ca-doped BaCeO$_3$, we identify the synergistic roles of small-radius, high-electronegativity A-site dopants in governing proton transport and chemical stability in perovskite electrolytes. We show that the higher electronegativity of A-site dopant weakens the A-O ionic bonding, facilitating oxygen-vacancy formation and enhancing proton uptake by increasing the basicity. This weakened A-O interaction also suppresses the formation of impurity phases and reduces the adsorption strength of acidic gases such as CO$_2$ and SO$_2$. The lattice contraction induced by the smaller ionic radius improves thermal stability and can enhance proton diffusion in systems where proton transfer is the rate-limiting step. Furthermore, we find that Ca surface segregation can mitigate grain-boundary resistance effects. Our results demonstrate the advantages of A-site Ca doping in Ba-based electrolytes, clarify the mechanisms by which small-radius, high-electronegativity dopants influence proton transport and chemical stability, and provide guidance for the design of high-performance proton-conducting electrolytes.

infographic.key_insight: Small-radius, high-electronegativity A-site dopants like Ca in BaCeO3 can simultaneously improve proton transport and chemical stability by weakening A–O bonding, increasing vacancy/proton uptake, and reducing gas adsorption.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A-site doping provides a practical design lever for proton-conducting Ba-based electrolytes, potentially enabling more durable solid oxide fuel cell materials with lower grain-boundary resistance.
method: First-principles calculations on Ca-doped BaCeO3.
Mechanistic analysis linking A-site electronegativity and ionic radius to vacancy formation, proton uptake, and gas adsorption.
Assessment of lattice contraction, impurity-phase suppression, and surface segregation effects.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports computational evidence that Ca doping weakens A–O interactions, lowers adsorption strength for CO2/SO2, and can improve proton diffusion when proton transfer is rate-limiting.
infographic.watch_item: The benefits may depend on doping level, operating conditions, and whether Ca segregation or lattice contraction introduces trade-offs in real microstructures.
infographic.paper_title: Role of small-radius and high-electronegativity A-Site dopants in enhancing proton transport and stability of perovskite electrolytes

title: Synthesis of the Elusive Bulk Iodide Double-Perovskite Semiconductor, Cs2AgBiI6: Microcrystals and Photoconductive Films
authors: Faris Horani, Nicolas Nguyen, Carmelita Ro-Mendez, Nicholas J. Adams, Daniel R. Gamelin
abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) iodide double-perovskite (elpasolite) semiconductors have attracted interest as potential lead-free metal-halide absorber layers for solar applications. Although studied extensively by computational methods, they have remained largely inaccessible synthetically, consistent with their predicted thermodynamic instability. Here, we report the first synthesis of bulk Cs2AgBiI6, demonstrating both microcrystalline and thin-film forms. Microcrystalline powders of Cs2AgBiI6 were prepared via anion exchange from phase-pure Cs2AgBiBr6 microcrystals. The resulting iodide elpasolite shows broad absorption throughout the visible with a 1.70 +/- 0.05 eV optical bandgap and near-infrared photoluminescence centered at 1.03 eV. We identify the elimination of trace moisture in bulk Cs2AgBiBr6 as the critical factor enabling complete halide exchange and isolation of bulk Cs2AgBiI6 with phase purity. In inert atmosphere, microcrystalline Cs2AgBiI6 shows no decomposition when stored for months at room temperature or heated to ~70 °C, and it appears equally stable in dry air. Building upon these insights, we then demonstrate the preparation of phase-pure Cs2AgBiI6 films by flash thermal evaporation of Cs2AgBiBr6 followed by anion exchange. Photoconductivity measurements on such Cs2AgBiI6 films demonstrate photocarrier generation and transport, marking the first optoelectronic measurement on this elusive 3D iodide double perovskite.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that phase-pure bulk Cs2AgBiI6, a long-predicted but elusive lead-free iodide double perovskite, can be synthesized in both microcrystal and thin-film form by carefully controlling moisture during halide exchange.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This establishes a new non-toxic absorber candidate for perovskite solar and optoelectronic devices, with demonstrated stability and measurable photoconductive response.
method: Prepare phase-pure Cs2AgBiBr6 microcrystals as the bromide precursor
Remove trace moisture to enable complete anion exchange from Br to I
Form films by flash thermal evaporation of Cs2AgBiBr6 followed by anion exchange
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a 1.70 ± 0.05 eV optical bandgap, near-infrared photoluminescence at 1.03 eV, months-long room-temperature stability, and photoconductivity in phase-pure films.
infographic.watch_item: The material is still an early-stage absorber with no device-level solar-cell efficiency shown, so synthesis reproducibility and film quality will be key implementation risks.
infographic.paper_title: Synthesis of the Elusive Bulk Iodide Double-Perovskite Semiconductor, Cs2AgBiI6: Microcrystals and Photoconductive Films

title: Understanding surface potential dynamics of passivated perovskites via Kelvin Probe Force Microscopy
authors: Rehmat Sood-Goodwin, Xue-Li Cao, Benjamin C. Kinvig, Robert D. J. Oliver, Yen-Hung Lin, Nic Mullin
abstract: Molecular passivation has become central to reducing photovoltage losses in metal-halide perovskite solar cells, but its electronic action is still often inferred from device-level metrics rather than directly resolved at the nanoscale. Here, we use amplitude-modulated Kelvin probe force microscopy to examine how [3-(2-aminoethylamino)propyl]trimethoxysilane (AEAPTMS) modifies the surface potential and photovoltage dynamics of mixed-cation, mixed-halide perovskite thin films. AEAPTMS homogenises the dark contact potential difference (CPD), narrowing its distribution from ~45.7 to ~14.6 mV without obvious morphological changes. Under illumination, passivated films show a larger steady-state surface photovoltage (SPV) and faster stabilisation, with the SPV increasing from ~345 to ~417 mV and the stabilisation time constant decreasing from ~840 to ~470 s. Wavelength-dependent SPV further indicates reduced sub-bandgap electronic disorder. By separating grain-boundary and grain-interior contributions, we show that AEAPTMS suppresses grain-boundary potential barriers, linking amino-silane passivation to a more homogeneous and stable carrier landscape.

infographic.key_insight: AEAPTMS amino-silane passivation makes mixed-halide perovskite surfaces electronically more uniform, reducing grain-boundary barriers and improving photovoltage dynamics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests molecular passivation can directly improve perovskite solar cell stability and voltage output by smoothing surface potential landscapes at the nanoscale.
method: Amplitude-modulated Kelvin probe force microscopy measured dark CPD and light-induced SPV on perovskite thin films.
Compared passivated vs unpassivated films to quantify surface-potential homogeneity and photovoltage stabilization.
Used wavelength-dependent SPV and grain-boundary/grain-interior separation to probe sub-bandgap disorder and local barriers.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports CPD distribution narrowing from ~45.7 to ~14.6 mV, SPV increasing from ~345 to ~417 mV, and stabilization time decreasing from ~840 to ~470 s after AEAPTMS treatment.
infographic.watch_item: These results are based on thin-film nanoscale measurements, so translating the observed surface improvements into full device performance requires careful validation under operating conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Understanding surface potential dynamics of passivated perovskites via Kelvin Probe Force Microscopy

title: What enables GaOx as hole transport layer for a 16 percent 1.0 eV CuInSe2 Bottom Cells with VOC above 550 mV?
authors: Francesco Lodola, Zhuangyi Zhou, Boaz Koren, Saeed Bayat, Alessandro Magon, Yucheng Hu
abstract: Among the highly efficient photovoltaic technologies, that do not rely on epitaxy, only chalcopyrites have a bandgap tunable down to 1.00 eV, the ideal for tandem applications. This is obtained with a pure CuInSe2 absorber without Ga. GaOx has been shown to be an efficient hole transport layer that prevents recombination at the metallic back contact. On the other hand, GaOx has proven detrimental, when it forms on In containing transparent back contacts in bifacial solar cells. Here, we investigate the conditions that make the GaOx layer conductive. We employ a GaOx hole transport layer that is formed through ion exchange during co-evaporation of the low band gap absorber layer. We find that no additional Cu is needed, and that Na is not necessary for a conductive GaOx. Nor did we find a systematic influence of oxygen flow during the sputtering process of the oxide layer. The GaOx layer is partly crystalline. The optimized passivating hole transport layer enables a CuInSe2 bottom solar cell, without any addition of Ag or heavy alkalis, with an active area efficiency above 16% and a record-certified open-circuit voltage VOC of 552meV

infographic.key_insight: A conductive, partly crystalline GaOx hole transport layer can be formed in situ during CuInSe2 co-evaporation, enabling strong back-contact passivation and high-voltage 1.0 eV bottom cells without heavy alkali or Ag additions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This work identifies a practical route to improve tandem-ready CuInSe2 bottom-cell performance by stabilizing the rear interface while preserving a low bandgap absorber and achieving record-level open-circuit voltage.
method: Formed GaOx through ion exchange during co-evaporation of the absorber layer.
Tested whether Cu addition, Na presence, and oxygen-flow conditions affect GaOx conductivity.
Evaluated device performance in CuInSe2 solar cells with the optimized rear passivating contact.
infographic.evidence_signal: The optimized devices achieved active-area efficiency above 16% and a record-certified VOC of 552 mV for a 1.0 eV CuInSe2 bottom cell.
infographic.watch_item: The conductive behavior appears tied to specific GaOx formation conditions and partial crystallinity, so transferability to other back-contact stacks or deposition recipes may be limited.
infographic.paper_title: What enables GaOx as hole transport layer for a 16 percent 1.0 eV CuInSe2 Bottom Cells with VOC above 550 mV?

title: Robustness of Deep Learning Models for PV Power Forecasting under NWP Forecast Errors: A Spatiotemporal and Physically Interpretable Analysis
authors: Dandan Chen, Yan Zhao, Xuepeng Chen
abstract: Engineering use of AI forecasting models requires not only high nominal accuracy but also predictable behavior under uncertain inputs. In photovoltaic (PV) forecasting, this requirement is especially challenging because numerical weather prediction (NWP) errors are temporally correlated, state dependent, and physically coupled across variables. Existing evaluations, however, often rely on perfect forecast assumptions or simplistic perturbations that do not reflect these characteristics. This study presents a physically constrained robustness evaluation framework based on simulation, using virtual PV power as a controlled response variable to isolate the propagation of input uncertainty from confounders at the plant level. Six representative machine learning and deep sequence models, including PatchTST, GRU, N-HITS, and LightGBM, are evaluated under dynamic NWP perturbations with heteroscedasticity modulated by clear-sky conditions and Erbs reconstruction that preserves radiation consistency. The results show that sequence models provide stronger noise filtering and temporal resilience than a strong tabular baseline under medium to high disturbance regimes. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Integrated Gradients (IG) further support a feature reallocation tendency at the case level, in which predictive reliance shifts from corrupted future forecasts toward more stable historical observations and deterministic physical priors. A Pareto analysis of accuracy under clean conditions, robustness, and computational latency then translates these findings into engineering implications for robustness assessment and model selection under forecast uncertainty.

infographic.key_insight: Deep sequence models are more robust than tabular baselines for PV power forecasting when NWP inputs are noisy, because they better filter temporal disturbances and shift attention toward stable historical and physical cues.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For PV forecasting systems, robustness should be selected alongside nominal accuracy and latency, especially when forecasts will operate under realistic NWP uncertainty rather than idealized inputs.
method: Physically constrained simulation using virtual PV power to isolate input-uncertainty effects.
Dynamic NWP perturbations with clear-sky–modulated heteroscedastic errors and Erbs-based radiation consistency.
Compare six ML/DL models with SHAP, Integrated Gradients, and Pareto analysis of accuracy, robustness, and latency.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports evaluation of six models under temporally correlated, state-dependent NWP perturbations and finds sequence models outperform a strong tabular baseline at medium to high disturbance levels.
infographic.watch_item: Robustness results are simulation-based and depend on the realism of the injected NWP error model, so transfer to a specific plant or region may require recalibration.
infographic.paper_title: Robustness of Deep Learning Models for PV Power Forecasting under NWP Forecast Errors: A Spatiotemporal and Physically Interpretable Analysis
